stories.summary: Amit's friend Vaishnav told him about a schoolboy who, on a festival day (possibly Diwali), rigged a chain of timed firecrackers across multiple floors of the school building. He timed them so each firecracker went off in sequence — fourth floor, then third, then second — sending the teachers running uselessly up and down the stairs as each new explosion went off elsewhere. Amit's reaction: 'These are the future of our country. This is innovation.' Channelled correctly, that creative-mischievous energy is exactly what builds great firms.
stories.insight: Latent entrepreneurial energy in India is enormous; the question is whether the system channels it into high-productivity firms or into rent-seeking and scams. The same kid who rigs firecrackers becomes either a global engineer or a Bihar telemarketer scammer depending on the institutional environment around him.

stories.topic: They Stole a Bridge in Bihar
stories.summary: Amit relays from his Seen and Unseen episode with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand: in Bihar, an entire 60-foot bridge was stolen — one day there was a bridge, the next day there wasn't. Even more surreally, the bridge had been stolen after a particular river patch with water running through it had also been stolen earlier. Many of the big telemarketing scams operating in India are run out of a couple of towns in Bihar.
stories.insight: It is the same imagination, manpower, and risk-tolerance that, with better incentives and rule of law, would compete with anyone in the world. The diagnosis isn't 'Indians are crooks' — it's that the institutional environment is steering exceptional human capital toward fraud and theft instead of high-productivity firms.

stories.topic: The Ricardian Rebuttal to Subsidising Software's Effect on Manufacturing
stories.summary: When Indian companies started exporting software successfully, the rupee appreciated, which damaged Indian manufacturing exports — what economists call 'Dutch disease.' This sounds like a problem, but Ajay frames it as Ricardian comparative advantage at work: the country specialises in what it does best, and that specialisation contains hardship for low-productivity firms doing things the country isn't good at. They will exit, those goods will be imported, imports and exports will move together, and the trade gap is just a small capital-account number — not a meaningful target.
stories.insight: The right macro frame is not 'maximise exports vs. minimise imports' but 'specialise where you are productive, import what you are not.' Worrying about the trade deficit as a scoreboard is mostly a fallacy of composition — what is good for one company doesn't scale to a national policy goal.

stories.topic: Sundar Pichai's Test for Indian Openness
stories.summary: Ajay cites Sundar Pichai saying it will be a great day for India when a Bangladeshi immigrant becomes the CEO of Infosys — just as Pichai, an Indian immigrant, became CEO of Google. Today, Satya Nadella, Pichai, and many others run top American firms with no friction; the appointment is treated as ordinary. India is nowhere near that — we would culturally resent a foreigner running TCS or Infosys.
stories.insight: The fact that so many top American companies have Indian-origin CEOs speaks to the greatness of America, not (yet) of India. Openness to foreign talent at the highest levels is itself a measure of a country's seriousness about productivity over identity.

stories.summary: Ajay (drawing on Lant Pritchett) recounts the political bargain in South Korea between the government and eight or ten big business houses (chaebols): in form it was crony capitalism, but the deal was that the government would create conditions for these firms to export. Once exports became the metric, the government couldn't help its champions by screwing American competitors — protectionism is useless against foreign markets. So the entire energy of public policy turned pro-productivity.
stories.insight: Even crony capitalism can be productive if the cronyism is conditioned on exports. The key institutional move isn't picking winners — it's choosing a metric (exports) that protectionism cannot fake, which forces the whole state-business relationship in a healthy direction.

stories.topic: Mr. Capital is the Most Important Input to a Steel Mill
stories.summary: An engineering view of a steel factory lists iron ore, coal, machines, and labour as inputs. A business view recognises the elephant in the room: capital. The capital cost per ton of steel is larger than any of those other inputs combined. So the most important question for an Indian steel mill's competitiveness is not where it gets coal but whether it can match the price of capital that Korean or Japanese mills get — which means going all-in on foreign equity and foreign debt, because Indian capital is more expensive (poor country, bad financial system).
stories.insight: If you are loyal to the firm's productivity, you must be loyal to the cheapest inputs — including capital. Treating foreign capital as foreign and therefore suspect is as silly as refusing to import the best coal. The cost of nationalist 'pride' on capital shows up directly in your unit economics.

stories.topic: The Indian Software Industry Didn't Wait for the State
stories.summary: TCS, Infosys, and the other heroes of Indian software didn't wait for the government to build engineering colleges that would graduate a million programmers a year. They went ahead and solved their own problems. Their growth was an act of bypassing the state altogether, which is why they could become world-class even within a generally bad institutional environment.
stories.insight: The path forward for Indian firms is not 'wait for the state to fix electricity, education, and law' (those are 25-year journeys at best) but to internationalise now, minimising state interfaces and competing on world markets where the Indian government can't help them and can't be weaponised against them.

stories.summary: Amit, building on a rant against the limits of randomised controlled trials in development economics, mocks the trivial questions some RCTs answer ('do treated mosquito nets help prevent malaria?') and jokes that someone is probably running an RCT on whether people perceive a yellow shirt as brighter than a black shirt. The deeper complaint: the RCT-only methodology has captured prestige in development economics, leaving the truly important questions (what makes high-productivity firms emerge?) under-studied because they cannot be randomised.
stories.insight: Methodological purity becomes intellectual cowardice when it lets you study only trivial questions. The 'RCT Nazi' is the empirical equivalent of looking under the streetlight for your keys — you do good clean work, but on the wrong question.

recommendations.item: In Defense of Globalization
recommendations.creator: Jagdish Bhagwati
recommendations.context: Bhagwati's classic defence of free trade and openness as forces for good.
recommendations.reason: Amit's headline recommendation for the episode. Bhagwati's argument — that globalisation has been the greatest poverty-reduction engine in human history and that protectionism harms the very people it claims to defend — is the natural reading partner for Ajay's case for firm internationalisation.

recommendations.item: Graduating to Globalisation: A Study of Southern Multinationals
recommendations.creator: Dilek Demirbas, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The paper whose title supplies the episode's name; it studies how firms from developing countries (especially India) become outbound multinationals.
recommendations.reason: The original source for the episode's central frame: that the journey from a domestic firm to a global firm is graduated and goes through multiple modes — exports, imports, FDI in and out, foreign capital, foreign labour — that all reinforce each other.

recommendations.item: India's Financial Globalisation
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and Ila Patnaik
recommendations.context: A survey paper on how India has integrated (and failed to integrate) into world capital markets.
recommendations.reason: Background for the 'Mr. Capital' argument — why foreign capital is structurally cheaper for Indian firms, and why interfering with capital-account flows is interfering with Indian firm productivity.

recommendations.item: Export Versus FDI with Heterogeneous Firms
recommendations.creator: Elhanan Helpman, Marc J. Melitz and Stephen R. Yeaple
recommendations.context: A foundational paper in modern trade theory on how firms self-select into exporting versus building foreign subsidiaries.
recommendations.reason: The theoretical scaffolding for Ajay's claim that exports and FDI are not substitutes on a menu but complementary modes of internationalisation that emerge naturally from heterogeneity in firm productivity.

recommendations.item: Exporting and Firm Performance: Evidence from India
recommendations.creator: Apoorva Gupta, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Empirical study using Indian firm-level data on the relationship between exporting and firm productivity.
recommendations.reason: Direct evidence for the episode's central claim — that exporting is not just a sales channel but a journey to higher productivity, with the data drawn from Indian firms.

recommendations.item: Export vs FDI in Services
recommendations.creator: Rudrani Bhattacharya, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: An extension of the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple framework to services rather than goods.
recommendations.reason: Important for the Indian case because so much of India's internationalisation has been in services (software, BPO) rather than manufacturing — different dynamics for setting up abroad versus exporting from India.

recommendations.item: Motivations for Capital Controls and Their Effectiveness
recommendations.creator: Radhika Pandey, Gurnain K. Pasricha, Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Empirical paper on why countries impose capital controls and whether those controls actually work.
recommendations.reason: Speaks to the policy thread of the episode: India's anti-internationalisation reflexes (RBI, ED, capital controls) hurt firms more than they help, and the empirical case for the controls is much weaker than the political enthusiasm for them.

recommendations.item: Did the Indian Capital Controls Work as a Tool of Macroeconomic Policy?
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Targeted empirical analysis of India's capital controls.
recommendations.reason: Companion piece showing that the Indian state's capital-control machinery is largely ineffective — the political-economy rationale for the controls is far stronger than the macroeconomic one.

recommendations.item: Capital Account Openness in India and a Comparison with China: Then versus Now
recommendations.creator: Nidhi Aggarwal, Sanchit Arora and Rajeswari Sengupta
recommendations.context: Comparative analysis of how India and China have opened (and not opened) their capital accounts over time.
recommendations.reason: Important comparative work showing how the two large Asian economies diverge in their openness to foreign capital, and what India can learn — even after China's recent retreat under Xi.

recommendations.item: Determinants of Trade Misinvoicing
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik, Abhijit Sen Gupta and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Empirical paper on illicit financial flows disguised as trade — the problem of fake invoices used to move money across borders.
recommendations.reason: Demonstrates that capital controls and anti-foreigner regulations create their own evasion economy: when legal cross-border activity is too painful, firms route around it through misinvoicing.

recommendations.item: The Investment Technology of Foreign and Domestic Institutional Investors in an Emerging Market
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Empirical study comparing how foreign institutional investors and domestic institutions actually invest in Indian markets.
recommendations.reason: Evidence for the 'Mr. Capital' argument: foreign investors bring not just capital but a different and often superior investment technology, which shows up in returns and behaviour.

recommendations.item: Foreign Investors under Stress: Evidence from India
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Nirvikar Singh
recommendations.context: How foreign investors actually behave during financial stress episodes in India.
recommendations.reason: A counter to the standard fear that foreign capital is 'hot money' that will flee in a crisis — the empirical record is more nuanced and the policy implications are different from the protectionist instinct.

recommendations.item: Foreign Currency Borrowing by Indian Firms: Towards a New Policy Framework
recommendations.creator: Ila Patnaik, Ajay Shah and Nirvikar Singh
recommendations.context: A policy paper on how Indian firms should be allowed to borrow in foreign currencies.
recommendations.reason: Directly relevant to the steel-mill example: Indian firms competing globally need access to cheaper foreign debt capital, and the current policy framework is unnecessarily restrictive.

recommendations.item: From Domestic to Global Asset Pricing
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A paper on how asset pricing changes as a country integrates into world capital markets.
recommendations.reason: Theoretical underpinning for why financial globalisation lowers the cost of capital — Indian firms become priced against a global rather than a local risk-free rate.

recommendations.item: Instant Cross-Border Payments vs. Current Account Inconvertibility
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah and Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah
recommendations.context: A paper on the tension between the modern reality of instant global payments and India's still-restrictive capital-account framework.
recommendations.reason: Captures the absurdity of the current Indian situation — global payment rails make money flow in milliseconds while the regulatory regime still treats every cross-border transaction as suspicious.

recommendations.item: Cross-Border Activities in India Need More Freedom, Not Less
recommendations.creator: Pratik Datta and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: A policy argument against tightening rules on Indian firms operating abroad.
recommendations.reason: Direct prescription for the policy person in this episode: the Indian state's instinct that 'foreign engagement is suspicious' is a major drag on firm productivity, and the solution is liberalisation, not more compliance theatre.

recommendations.item: Three Great Leaps by Firms (Episode 22, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: The first EIE episode focused entirely on firms.
recommendations.reason: Amit frames this episode as part of a continuing body of work; episode 22 is the foundation, on three firms that surprised them in how they changed.

recommendations.item: How Family Firms Evolve (Episode 34, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on the evolution of Indian family-run firms.
recommendations.reason: Part of the larger arc on how Indian firms have evolved over the last thirty years — Amit calls this 'novel and original thought' that should be standard in universities but isn't.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on how Indian firms have moved from imperial to adaptive organisational forms.
recommendations.reason: The third pillar in the firms arc — about how organisational structure inside firms has had to evolve to handle the diversity of India.

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: Amit's deep-dive episode with Lant Pritchett, including his critique of development economics and the South Korean chaebol story.
recommendations.reason: The conversation that informs both the Pritchett-style chaebol bargain framing in this episode and Amit's promised future EIE on 'everything wrong with development economics.'

recommendations.item: Economic Learnings of India for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Bihar (Episode 345, The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Mohit Satyanand and Kumar Anand
recommendations.context: Amit's Seen and the Unseen episode on Bihar with Satyanand and Anand.
recommendations.reason: Source of the 'they stole a bridge' and 'they stole a pond' anecdotes that Amit uses to illustrate the same latent entrepreneurial energy that, channelled correctly, builds great firms.

recommendations.item: They Stole a Bridge. They Stole a Pond.
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit's column on the Bihar bridge and pond thefts.
recommendations.reason: Companion piece that crystallises the point — these are not just funny news items but a window into both the failure of state capacity and the unbounded creative energy beneath it.

recommendations.item: The Brave New Future of Electricity (Episode 40, Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: EIE episode on Indian electricity policy.
recommendations.reason: Background for Ajay's aside in this episode that fixing Indian electricity is a 25-year journey — firms cannot wait for it, they must internationalise now.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic: The Art and Science of Economic Policy
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Kelkar and Shah's book on economic policy frameworks.
recommendations.reason: Referenced as the foundation for the public-policy lens on this episode — every public-policy question reduces to: how do we create the conditions in which India's people come together into sophisticated, high-productivity firms?

core_ideas.concept: Firm Productivity Is the Necessary and Sufficient Condition for Becoming an Advanced Economy
core_ideas.explanation: The development question is not poverty, not redistribution, not GDP per capita as a target — it is firm productivity. An advanced economy is one where the labour force produces a lot per working hour, and that production happens inside firms. If a quarter of the Indian working-age population were employed in firms playing at global frontiers of productivity, India would be a developed country. Everything else — education, health, infrastructure — is an input into that, but firm productivity is the touchstone. Ajay contrasts this with Saudi Arabia or Qatar, which have high incomes from pulling gas out of the ground but have not become productive societies.
core_ideas.quote: Getting to high productivity firms is the necessary and sufficient condition of becoming an advanced economy.

core_ideas.concept: Internationalisation (I18N) Has Six Modes That Reinforce Each Other
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay catalogues six modes of firm internationalisation: (1) imported raw materials and machines, (2) exporting goods and services, (3) inbound foreign capital — equity (portfolio to FDI) and debt, (4) outbound FDI, (5) foreign workers in the firm, (6) foreign technology. Old policy thinking treated these as a menu — pick exports, refuse FDI, etc. The modern view is that they are deeply interconnected: each one feeds the others. Foreign workers bring vendor relationships that enable imports; foreign capital brings board members who help with outbound FDI; outbound presence creates local sales that show up as foreign revenue, not exports. The right metric is internationalisation as a whole, not exports alone.
core_ideas.quote: On any of the six dimensions, you push forward in one dimension, it'll end up helping the other dimensions.

core_ideas.concept: Why Exporting Is Magic — The Political-Economy Argument
core_ideas.explanation: Exporting is precious not just because it expands the market but because it transforms domestic political economy. Domestic firms inevitably weaponise the state against each other (regulations, tax raids, anti-foreigner protection); the state in a developing country is too available for capture. But Infosys cannot lobby the Indian government to make it easier to sell into Germany. The only way to win in a foreign market is productivity. So exporting redirects the firm's entire internal energy from rent-seeking to building better products — it forces good behaviour even in a bad institutional environment. This is the Bhagwati-Srinivasan-Krueger insight, and it is the theoretical core of the episode.
core_ideas.quote: Exporting is a higher place. Exporting is a higher ground where those kinds of bad things don't happen.

core_ideas.concept: Fake Exports — The PLI and Exchange-Rate Trap
core_ideas.explanation: There are two toxic ways governments can simulate the form of exports without the substance. One is direct subsidy (Production-Linked Incentives, or PLI schemes, give money to exporters). The other is exchange-rate distortion — at 100 rupees a dollar instead of 80, Indian goods are artificially cheap abroad and inefficient firms can export. In both cases the country gets a billion dollars of exports on paper but does not get the underlying high-productivity firms that exporting was supposed to build. Means and ends become confused; the metric is hit but the goal is missed.
core_ideas.quote: You on paper got your exporting, but you didn't actually get what it was all about.

core_ideas.concept: Modern Firms Are Multinational — 50% of Trade Happens Within Firms
core_ideas.explanation: A full 50% of global trade is intra-firm — engine made in Brazil, shipped to Madras, assembled into a car, sold in America, all inside one corporation. Modern production is geographically distributed across the world, with firms looking at the whole world as a list of opportunities and ignoring lines on maps. This means you cannot 'like exporting and dislike multinationals' — they are one and the same phenomenon. To be a serious exporter is to be deep inside the world of MNCs, both inbound and outbound. The Fernandes-era hostility to multinationals is incoherent with any modern theory of trade.
core_ideas.quote: A wise firm, a smart firm, a sensible firm will not care about lines on borders.

core_ideas.concept: Mr. Capital — The Most Important Input Is Usually Invisible
core_ideas.explanation: An engineering view of a steel mill counts iron ore, coal, machines, and labour as inputs. The economics view names the elephant in the room: capital, whose unit cost per ton of steel exceeds the others combined. To be globally competitive, an Indian steel mill must match the cost of capital faced by Korean and Japanese rivals — which means foreign equity and foreign debt, because Indian capital is structurally more expensive (poor country, weak financial system). It is as silly to refuse foreign capital on patriotic grounds as it would be to refuse the best imported coal.
core_ideas.quote: Mr. Capital is the most important input provider to make a profitable steel mill.

core_ideas.concept: Internationalisation as a Fast and Frugal Heuristic
core_ideas.explanation: For investors and boards facing principal-agent and asymmetric-information problems, internationalisation provides a remarkably hard-to-fake metric of firm quality. A domestic Indian firm's success could be productivity, or it could be regulatory capture, blocked competitors, captured monopolies — you have to dig in. But a firm that sells in the European Union or the United States has passed a market test no Indian state can rig. Boards should demand metrics on every mode: export-to-sales ratio, FDI, foreign workers, foreign capital, imported inputs. These are deeply connected to productivity and almost impossible to fake.
core_ideas.quote: Show me that you are able to go sell in those countries. Then I know you are a high productivity firm.

core_ideas.explanation: There is a deep cultural pattern across the Indian state — SEBI, RBI, ED, Income Tax, GST, Ministry of Company Affairs — that treats foreign engagement as inherently suspicious. A Swiss bank account, a Dubai entity, a foreign subsidiary, even foreign travel are seen as bad things. The compliance burden is so heavy that smaller firms simply give up on international activity. This pushes India's globalisation entirely into the largest firms (who can absorb the compliance cost) and freezes out the next generation. It is the Indian state actively interfering with India's own emergence.
core_ideas.quote: If you fly to London, within 10 minutes you will get a bank account opened. You'd suffer the misery of a foreigner coming to India trying to open a bank account.

core_ideas.concept: Capitalism as an Ennobling Force — The Stigler Argument
core_ideas.explanation: George Stigler's insight: the capitalist who discriminates against a chosen minority is harming herself. In a competitive market, the most successful firms are the most meritocratic — they care about getting things done. Discrimination is a self-imposed tax on talent and is therefore selected against by competition. So great firms have a wonderful progressive social character: they bring people into voluntary contracts and 'double thank-you moments' across racial, religious, and national lines. Capitalism done right is anti-coercive and anti-discriminatory by structural necessity.
core_ideas.quote: Capitalism is an ennobling force in the way it brings together people into voluntary contracts.

core_ideas.concept: The Indian-Environment Trap — Why Domestic Success Is Bad Training
core_ideas.explanation: Beyond the political-economy problem, there is a subtler harm in being a domestic Indian firm. The Indian regulatory environment is so quirky — UPI monopolies, UID-AI, peculiar SEBI and RBI rules, a government-monopoly payment system — that firms which become deeply embedded in it learn skills that don't transfer. A payment system optimised for India's regulatory landscape is useless in the UK or Germany. So domestic Indian success can produce 'dwarves' — firms that look strong locally but cannot make the cognitive jump to a market without those peculiarities. The peculiarity of the local environment becomes a barrier to global graduation.
core_ideas.quote: The peculiarities of the domestic Indian environment are harming domestic firms.

core_ideas.concept: The Three Categories of Indian IT Firms (Nitin Pai's Classification)
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay relays Nitin Pai's classification, applied to internationalisation theory. (1) Old software services firms (TCS, Infosys, Wipro) — service exporters, market-tested. (2) SaaS firms — pure product companies that are essentially 100% exports. (3) Domestically-oriented firms. The first two categories are structurally safe and have an infinite market — they have already passed the test. The third is suspect: their success may be regulatory capture (PayPal blocked, UPI monopoly) rather than productivity, and their embedding in the Indian regulatory landscape makes them harder to graduate globally.
core_ideas.quote: Is UPI actually good, or did you do it through protectionism? Who knows.

core_ideas.concept: Patriotism vs. Nationalism in Firm Strategy
core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Ramachandra Guha's distinction (and Tagore's much older one): patriotism is loving your country and wanting it to win on a level playing field; nationalism is the chest-thumping, exclusionary, mediocre-protecting version. The toxic role of the state — protectionism, subsidies, exchange-rate manipulation, anti-foreigner policy — flows from nationalism, which is also the natural language of domestic firms (because it benefits them). A true patriot says: we have it in us to be as good as anyone in the world, let us compete and prove it. The nationalist says: shield me from competition, I want to be mediocre.
core_ideas.quote: Nationalism is the language of domestic firms.

core_ideas.concept: Get Out of the Way — The Minimal-State Stance for I18N
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's observation that runs through the policy section: almost everything Ajay prescribes is for the state to stop doing things — stop subsidising, stop manipulating exchange rates, stop blocking foreigners, stop torturing firms with compliance. The long-run state-building projects (electricity, education, courts) are 25-year journeys and cannot be waited on. In the meantime there is enough hunger and enough opportunity in India to produce tremendous progress purely by removing state interference with cross-border activity. The TCS-Infosys playbook of bypassing the state altogether is a template, not an exception.

core_ideas.concept: Don't Wait for the Indian State — The Firm-Level Strategic Imperative
core_ideas.explanation: Every Indian firm should ask itself a binary question: is my core skill 'fixing the Indian system' or 'being a competent firm'? If the latter, then exposure to the Indian regulatory and political landscape is a liability and should be minimised. International markets de-risk the firm from India's ups and downs and offer an effectively infinite growth runway. Even if you think you are clean, your competitors will eventually weaponise the Indian state against you — so it is safer to be far away from it. Internationalisation is not just a growth strategy; it is a defensive strategy.

core_ideas.concept: Development Economics Has Lost the Plot
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's running critique: mainstream development economics has drifted from the central question (how do poor countries become rich) into the easier and more philanthropic adjacent question (how do we transfer money to the poor). The four great development success stories of the post-1945 world — Taiwan, South Korea, Israel, Chile — are surprisingly under-studied; the field is captured by RCTs on poverty programmes that, even when they produce real results, cannot answer how to grow a high-productivity firm sector. The discipline has become 'an RCT Nazi' culture, blinkered by methodological purity. The serious researcher should refuse the blinkers and study what matters.
core_ideas.quote: I shall not allow my mind to be blinkered around one microscope.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit on the firecracker schoolboy story — that the kid timing explosions on every floor of his school to send teachers running up and down 'is the future of our country. This is innovation.'
Amit on the Bihar bridge theft: 'One day there was a bridge, it wasn't there. Only in Bihar.' And the bridge was stolen after a particular river patch had also been stolen earlier.
Amit, in role-play mode: 'I am a podcaster. What do I do? I'm kidding. Don't look at me like that.'

Amit on RCT triviality: imagining an RCT that asks 'do people perceive a yellow shirt to be brighter than a black shirt' — the kind of question development economists waste their lives on instead of studying how high-productivity firms emerge.

Ajay on the Indian state's compliance theatre: 'If you fly to London, within 10 minutes you will get a bank account opened. You'd suffer the misery of a foreigner coming to India trying to open a bank account.'

I18N — the computing-era abbreviation for 'internationalisation' (I followed by 18 letters then N), born from programmers tired of typing the long word as ASCII gave way to multi-language support. Ajay borrows it as the term for firm internationalisation.
George Stigler's argument that the capitalist who discriminates against a chosen minority is harming herself — invoked as the moral foundation of capitalism's anti-discriminatory tendency.

George Fernandes — the Janata-era Industries Minister famous for his obsessive hostility to multinational corporations, infamously ejecting IBM and Coca-Cola from India in 1977. Cited as the archetype of the now-disproved 'we don't need MNCs' position.

'Dutch disease' — the macroeconomic phenomenon where success in one export sector pushes up the exchange rate and damages other export sectors. Cited to defuse the worry that Indian software's appreciation of the rupee 'killed' Indian manufacturing.
Sundar Pichai's line that it will be a great day for India when a Bangladeshi immigrant becomes the CEO of Infosys — used to mark how far India has to travel on openness to foreign talent at the top.

Ramachandra Guha's distinction between patriotism (loving your country) and nationalism (toxic, exclusionary, chest-thumping, protectionist) — invoked to clarify that pro-globalisation is the patriotic position, not the unpatriotic one.
Bhagwati, T.N. Srinivasan, and Anne Krueger — the trio of trade economists whose work in the 1960s-70s established the political-economy case for export-led growth over import substitution.

The South Korean chaebols and Lant Pritchett's framing of them as a political bargain conditioned on exports — the canonical story Ajay invokes for how even cronyism can be productive if the metric forces good behaviour.
PLI (Production-Linked Incentive) schemes — the current Indian government's flagship subsidy programme for exporters, cited as the textbook 'fake exports' policy: form without substance.

Amit's running gag about the layered cast of metaphorical characters — 'you've already met Mr. Gas (in a previous episode), today you have met Mr. Capital' — building a recurring bestiary of inputs personified.
